at2w.correctionOf: An earlier reading the same day concluded 'redistribution, not creation' and set the verdict to do-not-extend. That was wrong, and it was wrong for a specific reason worth recording: it measured ONLY store-side sessions, because the site-side denominator was believed unreadable after GA4 528489903 returned 403. The 403 is real but it only affects the local MCP's OAuth identity. Production reads that exact property fine through the WIF service account brsg-analytics-reader@brsg-mcp, and the site's own /api/reports/outbound-clicks endpoint serves the per-page views and clicks. The denominator was one authenticated request away the whole time.
at2w.note: The hypothesis was that a hero door would lift conversion on lead-type pages from 0.95% to ~5%. Measured 7.24% on the four target pages - the bet BEAT its own conservative case. Critically, absolute clicks rose 6 -> 22 while views FELL 629 -> 304, so this is not a shrinking-denominator artifact: the pages did more with half the traffic. Site-wide affiliate clicks rose 69 -> 86 (+25%) over the same collapse.
at2w.theTension: Site-side clicks rose 25% but store-side sessions rose only 10% (49 -> 54). Two scoreboards, two answers. Commission is computed store-side, so the store number is the one that pays - but the site number is the one that isolates whether a design change worked. Track both and never quote one as the other. Part of the gap is the provider page giving back share: 39 clicks / 43.33% before, 28 clicks / 35.44% now.
at2w.theRealHeadline: Lead-type page views fell 629 -> 304 in two weeks, a >50% traffic collapse, which is the crawl transition still biting. Conversion work is now clearly succeeding on a shrinking base. That does not argue against more conversion work; it argues that conversion alone cannot outrun the traffic loss.

iterations.asset: components/header.tsx - persistent store door in the site header (utm_campaign=header-nav)
iterations.targetCluster: every page on the site; Header renders site-wide from app/(site)/layout.tsx
iterations.rationale: The 2026-09-02 scoreboard reading above found that 99% of May's and 91% of July's attributed store revenue came from a link in the RETIRED site's header, and that this site has no store link in its header at all. What stood in that slot was a blue 'Find Providers' button pointing at /providers - an internal page that duplicated the 'Providers' nav item three places to its left and converts at 0.61%, the worst on the site. The swap costs no navigation. This is a restoration of a placement with a measured record, not a new bet.
iterations.hypothesis: A header store door is PULLED by a reader who has decided to buy, where a banner under an article is PUSHED at one who has not. If posture is what separates $95/session from $1/session, restoring the header link should lift store-side sessions materially and should carry a higher revenue-per-session than cta-banner.

expected.basis: 1,107 site pageviews over the last 30d (GA4 528489903 via /api/reports/outbound-clicks). The header renders on all of them; the previous best single placement, /providers/aged-lead-store, reaches only 83. No click-rate forecast is stated on purpose - the point of this iteration is that clicks were the wrong unit. Judge it on store-side sessions and revenue under utm_campaign=header-nav in GA4 357329146.

iterations.killRule: REVISED 2026-09-09. Original rule: revert to the internal button if header-nav showed no store-side lift by 2026-09-16. That date is withdrawn, and the reason is a defect in the placement rather than a defence of it. Diagnosis on 2026-09-09 established that header-nav is STARVED, not broken: the live href carries all four UTMs, resolves 200 with zero redirects, and the destination preserves the query string. Two things made the 09-16 reading unsound. (1) UNDERPOWERED: 2 sessions over 7 days on a ~1,107 view/month base has a 95% interval of roughly 0.2-7.2 events; it cannot distinguish failure from noise. July's 96 sessions came from a site with an estimated 5-10x this traffic base. (2) THE PLACEMENT WAS HALF-BUILT: the button rendered only inside md:flex and inside the collapsed mobile menu, so below 768px roughly 40% of the audience had no header door at all unless they opened the hamburger. Verified live at 390px: hamburger only. Judging a placement that ~40% of readers could not see would have been a false negative. Fixed the same day - always-visible mobile bar button, breakpoint moved md -> xl so the nav stops clipping, and utm_content split three ways so desktop and mobile are separately attributable. New date gives a full 30 days on the repaired placement. Judge on click RATE against exposure, not absolute sessions, and note that July's figure was desktop-only so it is not like-for-like against a blended one.
iterations.concentrationFinding: 2026-10-05. The $7,734 that header-nav earned over the trailing 90 days was THREE orders, and one of them was $6,000 (2026-07-20) — 77.6% of the total. Verified directly against GA4 357329146 by transactionId: $6,000.00 / $986.40 / $747.60, all in July, all BEFORE the 2026-08-03 consolidation. Strip the outlier and the old door earned $22.82/session, statistically indistinguishable from the weekly newsletter's $20.98. The '$110/session' figure quoted in earlier sessions is one transaction wearing a rate's clothing, and it should not be used to size any decision.
iterations.audienceFinding: The old door's traffic was not readers converting. Across 2026-04 to 10-05, 159 of 174 header-nav sessions were RETURNING store users, and every order and every dollar came from returning users — zero revenue from new users, ever. 87% of the revenue landed on the store's /customers/login page at 12.8 pageviews and 7.7 form-starts per session: existing agedleadstore.com account holders using the retired site's header as a bookmark into a store they already bought from. The destination URL is byte-identical in both codebases (/all-lead-types/), so this is a property of WHO clicked, not of where the link pointed. That cohort left with the retired domain's direct traffic; rebuilding the button cannot recover it.
iterations.newDoorStatus: NOT failing — underpowered, exactly as the 2026-09-09 revision predicted. 40 sessions, 0 orders in 30 days. At the old door's own purchase rate (9/166 = 5.4%), zero purchases in 39 sessions happens 11.5% of the time by chance. The new door puts 16% of sessions into a cart against the old door's 24% (p~0.22, not distinguishable) and 230 pageviews across 37 sessions. Do not read 0 orders as a verdict. BLOCKER for the 2026-10-09 date: the revised rule says judge click RATE against exposure, and site-side GA4 528489903 returns 403 to the current credential, so exposure cannot be measured. The decision needs that access (the /website-audit WIF path) before it can be made honestly.
iterations.advanceDataAt20261005: Pulled 4 days early. Store-side GA4 357329146, 2026-09-01->10-05, by utm_content: header 24 sessions / 0 txn / $0.00; header-mobile 16 / 0 / $0.00; header-mobile-menu NO ROWS (the hamburger door has never been attributed a store session). Total header-nav 40 sessions, 0 transactions, $0.00 - which is 12.9% of the window's 310 affiliate sessions and 0% of its $3,269.40. For 2026-09-01->09-30: 30 sessions, 0 txn, $0.00. The revised rule asks for click rate against exposure, and that remains unmeasurable for the same reason recorded in newDoorStatus - exposure lives on site-side GA4 528489903, which 403s. Note 40 sessions with 0 orders is not yet statistically decisive on conversion alone (at the pre-consolidation 5.4% order rate, 0 of 40 has roughly an 11% chance), so the honest reading on 10-09 is a volume verdict, not a conversion one.
iterations.verdictBasis: Store-side GA4 357329146, 2026-09-01->10-05: header 24 sessions / 0 txn / $0.00, header-mobile 16 / 0 / $0.00 — 40 sessions total, 12.9% of the window's 310 affiliate sessions and 0% of its $3,269.40. The rule's own test (click rate against exposure) was NOT run and could not be: exposure needs site-side GA4 528489903, re-confirmed 403 on 2026-10-05.
iterations.theDecidingSplit: The 13 add-to-carts under the campaign are not this door's. Split the 40 sessions by landing page and the 13 that landed on /all-lead-types/ — where the door actually points — produced ZERO add-to-carts. All 13 carts came from the other 27, which landed deep in the storefront or on /customers/login: existing account holders whose sessions carry the tag by last-non-direct stickiness. The door shows no mid-funnel movement at all from the readers it sends, which is a stronger statement than '0 orders' and does not depend on the order-rate statistic.
iterations.whyNotKill: 0 orders on 40 sessions is not decisive on conversion (0-of-40 at the old 5.4% rate happens ~11% of the time), and the evidence does not separate 'header placement is worthless' from 'the marketing catalogue is a dead end' — the lead-type door shows the identical dead-end signature on a different placement, so the two are confounded. Killing now would remove the only site-wide path to the merchant while blaming the wrong variable. Changed instead: the dead third door (header-mobile-menu, zero store sessions ever, redundant with the always-visible bar button) removed 2026-10-05, and a new rule attached that measures only what store-side GA4 can produce.
iterations.killRule2026_11_09: Measured ONLY on store-side GA4 357329146, sessionMedium=affiliate, utm_campaign=header-nav, summed across utm_content header + header-mobile — the campaign total, not per-content, because 40 sessions in 35 days cannot support a per-content verdict. Two conditions over 2026-10-06 -> 11-09, both readable: (1) ORDERS — one or more store-side transactions attributed to header-nav. (2) CART — at least 3 add-to-carts from sessions whose landingPagePlusQueryString is the door's own destination /all-lead-types/. Condition 2 is the one that matters: it separates this door's own readers from the returning-account-holder sessions that carry the tag by last-non-direct stickiness. Fail both -> remove the placement. Pass either -> keep, re-measure 2026-12-09. Exposure, click rate, and anything requiring site-side GA4 528489903 are explicitly NOT part of this rule.

iterations.asset: app/(site)/page.tsx - HeroAffiliateDoor in the homepage hero
iterations.rationale: The homepage is the single highest-traffic page on the site - 398 views in 30d, more than the providers hub (163) and both calculators (142 + 93) combined - and it converts to the store at 0.5% (2 affiliate clicks). Its ONLY affiliate surface is <CtaBanner /> at line 450 of a 453-line file, i.e. the very bottom. The hero offers three buttons and every one is internal: /playbook, /providers, /price-index. That is precisely the defect HeroAffiliateDoor was built for - a reader at peak intent routed to another page on this site instead of to the merchant - and it is the same shape /providers had at 0.61% before iteration 4 took it to 3.68%.
iterations.hypothesis: The homepage hero is a weaker intent moment than a provider review or a calculator result, so the provider page's 29% is not the target. But 0.5% is a floor set by having no door at all, not by intent. Adding one door without touching the existing internal routes should behave like the providers hub did.

expected.basis: 398 views/mo at 0.5% today = 2 clicks. Modelling C at 3% - deliberately BELOW the 3.68% the providers hub reached and well below the 5% used for iterations 2 and 5, because homepage intent is broader and iteration 5 has already shown a door alone is not sufficient - gives ~12 clicks vs 2. At the $49/session the hero-door placement is currently earning, that is the largest single conversion gain available on the site without new traffic.

implementation.editorial: 'Get the Free Playbook' KEPT as the styled primary. It is the lead-magnet CTA that feeds the 2,464-contact lifecycle program, and demoting it to buy an affiliate click would trade a compounding asset for a one-off. The door carries its own affiliate disclosure, as everywhere else.

iterations.killRule: Kill if /  does not clear 2% by 2026-09-23. That is 4x today and still below the providers hub. If a door on the highest-traffic page cannot clear 2%, the door pattern has reached its limit on low-intent surfaces and the next iteration must buy intent rather than add placements.
iterations.deferral: DEFERRED 2026-09-15 (Bill): this kill date falls inside Bill's Europe trip (2026-09-17 to 09-30). Hold the measurement and the kill decision until the week of 2026-10-01. Nothing is reverted while he is away. The rule itself is unchanged.
iterations.verdictBasis: Decided on store-side revenue, NOT on the rule's stated metric. Store-side GA4 357329146, door-isolated by utm_content, 2026-09-01->10-05: homepage-hero/hero-door produced 1 session, 0 transactions, $0.00. Same figures for 2026-09-01->09-30.
iterations.statedMetricUnmeasurable: The rule's own test - door clicks divided by sessions on / - could not be computed, and the reason is worth keeping. (1) The numerator is not door-isolated: / carries three affiliate surfaces (this door, the bottom CtaBanner campaign=cta-banner, and the site header door, which renders on every page), and /api/reports/outbound-clicks attributes 7 affiliate clicks to the page as a whole. Its topLinks30d cannot split them because GA4 truncates linkUrl at 100 characters, cutting every row before the utm_campaign value. (2) The available denominator is screenPageViews (459), not sessions; sessions-per-page requires site-side GA4 528489903, which returns 403 'User does not have sufficient permissions for this property'. (3) The route serves only rolling 30d/90d windows, so neither the rule's 2026-09-23 date nor any custom window is obtainable. Sessions <= pageviews, so clicks/sessions >= 7/459 = 1.53%; the true rate could sit either side of the 2% bar and an upper-bound argument does NOT settle it. What settles it is that only 1 of those up-to-7 clicks reached the store carrying this door's tag, which puts the door's own click count near 1 in five weeks - below 2% on any denominator the page can have.
iterations.verdictApplied: Homepage instance removed 2026-10-05 from app/(site)/page.tsx. Deliberately NOT removed: the bottom CtaBanner (campaign=cta-banner), which this rule does not cover, and the shared HeroAffiliateDoor component, which earns on /providers and /lead-types. 'Get the Free Playbook' is untouched - it feeds the lifecycle program and that list compounds.
iterations.consequenceNowBinding: The rule named its own consequence: 'If a door on the highest-traffic page cannot clear 2%, the door pattern has reached its limit on low-intent surfaces and the next iteration must buy intent rather than add placements.' That now binds, and the window's full scoreboard says the same thing independently. Store-side GA4 357329146, 2026-09-01->10-05, all affiliate utm_sources: 310 sessions, 9 transactions, $3,269.40 (=$523.10 likely commission at REV_SHARE 0.2 x REALISATION 0.8). Every low-intent door earned $0.00: homepage 1 session, both calculator doors 0 sessions, header-nav 40 sessions. All 9 orders came from high-intent surfaces - providers-hub/hero-door 22 sessions -> 5 orders -> $545.00, and weekly-newsletter 2026-09-14-hero 13 sessions -> 3 orders -> $2,224.40, plus welcome-e3/top-cta 3 sessions -> 1 order -> $500.00. The newsletter alone is 68% of the revenue. Adding placements is finished as a lever; the next iteration buys or matches intent.

iterations.asset: data/guides.ts — the operator guide tier: Fresh-Consent Ladder, PEWC, warm-up sequence
iterations.targetCluster: /guides/* and the five reframed /blog/sms-templates-* and dialer posts
iterations.rationale: The site's promise is 'You Bought the Leads. Now Work Them.' The audit on 2026-09-09 found the library heavy on scripts and economics but missing the layer where an operator loses money, and worse, publishing SMS-template and dialer content that read as though inherited consent were sufficient while the doctrine saying otherwise sat inside a gated PDF. Keywords: 'prior express written consent' 150/mo KD 7 with no page on the site targeting it; the re-engagement cluster is 0-80/mo, so that half is an AEO and email-list play rather than an SEO one. Deliberately did NOT write a broad 'tcpa consent' article — /blog/tcpa-compliance-lead-buyers is a 3,642-word pillar already covering the 1:1 rule, revocation, ATDS, SMS, DNC, state mini-TCPAs and vendor diligence, and a second one would have split the site against itself.
iterations.hypothesis: Authority content converts differently from a product page. The bet is NOT that these guides produce affiliate clicks directly — it is that a reader who arrives on a consent question and finds the definitive answer subscribes, and that the cluster lifts the commercial pages it links to. Judge on assisted paths and email signups, not on clicks from the guide itself.

expected.basis: 'prior express written consent' is 150/mo at KD 7, and DR 2-3 sites rank top-10 in this niche, so ranking is a content question rather than an authority one. The warm-up guide targets terms with almost no volume and is written for citation and for the 6,086-person list instead.

implementation.tier: Code-backed data/guides.ts rather than the Sanity guide type, whose body is [block, image] only — no table, codeBlock, callout or step type. The tier emits FAQ JSON-LD and wires glossary auto-linking, neither of which /guides had before.
implementation.doctrine: Five off-doctrine posts reframed rather than unpublished (sms-templates-insurance-leads ranks position 27 on 88 impressions). Copy leads with the benefit — 'Text the people who asked you to' — not the prohibition.
implementation.glossary: Eight consent terms added to BOTH data/glossary-terms.ts and the Sanity glossaryTerm dataset; they are separate sources and the auto-linker reads only the second.

iterations.killRule: Measure 2026-10-10. Kill the per-lead-type guide expansion (13 more) if the three consent guides together have not produced either a measurable email-signup lift or a top-10 ranking for 'prior express written consent' by then. The doctrine pages stay regardless — they exist to stop the site contradicting itself and that value does not depend on traffic.

iterations.asset: data/guides.ts — pilot lead-type operator guides: final expense, life insurance, auto insurance
iterations.rationale: Bill's item 2 of the 2026-09-09 plan: per-lead-type guides covering who the customer is, what happened to the record while it aged, what they want now, the email sequence that earns renewed consent, tooling with honest limits, and the compliance boundary. Piloted on three verticals rather than all fourteen so the format is proven before ~35,000 words are committed. Auto carries real objections from a captive P&C buyer (2026-09-10): a 100-record batch scrubbed to 67 workable records, aged inventory carries no credit-back, and carrier CRMs strip purchased email addresses until contact and permission.
iterations.hypothesis: A vertical-specific operating guide converts a reader who arrived on a lead-type query better than the lead-type page alone, because it answers the question that decides whether they buy again — what to do with the batch. Judge on affiliate clicks from the guide and its lead-type page together, not on guide traffic.

expected.basis: Pilot verticals were chosen for low difficulty — final expense KD 1, auto KD 3, life KD 4 — with existing pages ranking 13–31. Search volume per guide is small (60–150/mo), so the read is conversion, not traffic.

implementation.tier: Static-first entries in data/guides.ts rendered by the /guides/[slug] fork ahead of the Sanity lookup, with FAQ JSON-LD and glossary auto-linking. Invariant tests enforce one consent ask per sequence, a stated limit on every tool, and no per-lead price.
implementation.glossary: Two terms added in both sources from the buyer conversation: lead spoilage and net usable rate.

iterations.killRule: Measure 2026-10-10. Do not write the other eleven lead-type guides if the three pilots, with their lead-type pages, have not cleared the lead-type pages' pre-launch affiliate click rate. Read via /api/reports/outbound-clicks. The three pilots stay live regardless.

iterations.asset: lib/newsletter/restock-offer.ts + app/api/cron/restock-offer — the monthly restock offer broadcast
iterations.targetCluster: The full Resend audience, including the purchaser contacts; sent first Thursday after the month's first Sunday
iterations.rationale: The only thing that ever asked a reader to buy again was a per-person journey — replenishment 21–90 days, win-back 90+ — and both are one-shot, so a buyer who finished them never saw an offer again. Store-side GA4 (357329146), Aug 1 – Sep 10: our affiliate link 137 sessions for $707, returning buyers landing on /customers/login 76 sessions for $8,693. The money in the store is repeat purchase, and nothing reached that group on a schedule.
iterations.hypothesis: A monthly, evergreen, pull-posture restock email reaches repeat buyers the per-person journeys stopped reaching, and earns attributed store revenue that the weekly newsletter does not. Six rotating editions keep the send from training the list to ignore it.

expected.basis: No baseline for a recurring offer exists. The one-off direct offer of 2026-09-10 is the nearest comparison. Read attributed revenue on utm_campaign=restock-offer against that send.

implementation.schedule: Drafts the first Sunday 14:00 UTC and mails Bill a preview with a one-click STOP link; sends the following Thursday 13:00 UTC after a 48-hour minimum window. Own archive (data/offer-archive), own campaign tag, own heartbeats watched by health-check.
implementation.firstCycle: Draft 2026-10-04, send 2026-10-08. Deliberately not September: the one-off offer mailed 2026-09-10.

iterations.killRule: Measure 2026-11-08, one month after the first send. Stop the program if the first edition earns no attributed store revenue on utm_campaign=restock-offer AND its unsubscribe rate exceeds the weekly newsletter's. Revenue with high unsubscribes, or unsubscribes normal with no revenue, is a copy problem to iterate on, not a kill.

iterations.killRule: Measure 2026-10-02. Do not repeat segmented product launches in this form if the two sends together earn no attributed store revenue on utm_campaign=mortgage-protection-launch AND the segment's unsubscribe rate exceeds the weekly newsletter's by more than double. iterations.result: KILLED. Both sends went out on time (announcement 2026-09-23, reminder 2026-09-25) to the 2,950-contact Life + Final Expense segment. Store-side GA4 357329146, 2026-09-16 to 10-04: utm_campaign=mortgage-protection-launch produced 23 sessions, 0 transactions, $0.00. Unsubscribes in the segment went from 0 at build to 40, which is 1.36% of recipients across two sends. Click-to-store was 0.8%. The kill rule's second test (unsubscribe rate against the newsletter's) could not be measured cleanly — the main list only exposes a cumulative 4.37% across its whole history, not a per-send rate — so this is called on revenue alone, which is unambiguous. In the SAME window the weekly newsletter earned 3 orders and $2,224.40 from 63 sessions, and welcome-e3 earned 1 order and $500.00 from 3 sessions. The list is not fatigued; this offer was simply not wanted.
iterations.lesson: A product launch is not a reason to email. The two sends that earn on this list are the weekly newsletter, which people opted in for, and the lifecycle steps that arrive when a buyer is already in motion. A partner announcement interrupts without either. Future partner news rides inside the newsletter, where it costs no extra send and no unsubscribes, rather than as its own broadcast.

measurementDebt.note: Three consecutive kill rules have now been written against metrics that require site-side GA4 528489903, which 403s to the credential this project can use: the header-nav rule (twice - it is why the 09-16 date was withdrawn and why 10-09 will also be a volume verdict), and the homepage hero door rule. Store-side GA4 357329146 is readable and door-isolated by utm_content, and our own /api/reports/outbound-clicks gives click counts by pagePath. RULE GOING FORWARD: write kill rules only against metrics those two sources can actually produce - store-side sessions, orders and revenue by utm_content, and click counts by pagePath - or fix the GA4 access first. A kill rule measured in a property we cannot read is a decision deferred by construction, and it has cost three deferrals already.
measurementDebt.correction: The original note overstated the blackout. Site-side GA4 528489903 does 403 to the GA4 MCP service account, but GET /api/reports/outbound-clicks reaches that same property successfully through the route own Workload Identity Federation path (lib/cron/google-auth.ts) - verified HTTP 200 on 2026-10-05. So per-page affiliate CLICK RATE (clicks / screenPageViews, by pagePath) IS measurable today and is a legitimate basis for a kill rule. What remains unmeasurable: sessions-per-page (the route exposes screenPageViews only), door-isolated click attribution on a page carrying more than one affiliate surface (GA4 truncates linkUrl at 100 chars, cutting every row before utm_campaign), and any custom window (the route serves rolling 30d/90d only). REVISED STANDING RULE: write kill rules against store-side GA4 357329146 by utm_content, or against /api/reports/outbound-clicks by pagePath click rate on a stated minimum view count. Never against a metric needing per-page SESSIONS, a custom date window, or click attribution on a page with multiple affiliate surfaces - those are the three that stranded the header-nav and homepage rules.
measurementDebt.update20261005: A fourth deferral was avoided rather than incurred. The header-nav 10-09 rule again could not be run (528489903 still 403s), but the verdict was taken on a readable substitute — store-side add-to-carts segmented by landingPagePlusQueryString, which separates a door's own readers from returning-account-holder sessions that carry the tag by last-non-direct attribution. That segmentation is the general fix for this class of rule, and both new rules (header 2026-11-09, lead-type hero-door-store 2026-11-09) are written against it. STANDING RULE, now demonstrated rather than asserted: a kill rule names store-side sessions/add-to-carts/orders/revenue by utm_content, or click counts by pagePath from /api/reports/outbound-clicks. Nothing else.
